introduced_concepts.definition: Extra food grown beyond what farming families need to stay alive, allowing a society to feed full-time weavers, builders, metalworkers, and scribes.
How a large group of people who are not all one family decides who gets to make shared rules, divide up scarce things like water and grain, and make sure everyone follows those rules.
A required share of a household's harvest or yearly workdays handed over so shared projects like flood dikes, canals, and public storehouses keep running.
A written running record that tracks what came in, what went out, and who owes what across months and years so managers do not rely on memory.
A written, witness-sealed agreement that a court can check and back up if a dispute breaks out later.
A single unified government that runs rules, taxes, and shared projects across an entire region of towns and villages rather than one independent city.
The shared trust that makes people accept a ruler's or government's authority as right and proper—through common beliefs, duties, and traditions—rather than obeying only out of fear.
A system in which a central authority collects crops, livestock, and labor taxes from across a region and hands them back out as rations, housing, tools, and care for shared projects.
Splitting one big project into specialized crews—such as quarrymen, boatmen, bakers, coppersmiths, and surveyors—so every team works faster and more accurately.
Planning and moving food, fuel, tools, and raw materials across long distances so thousands of workers at a site never run short.
